## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Migapotakajātaka* (Ja 372) is a Jātaka tale belonging to the Pali canonical collection, translated in modern sources under the English title *The Fawn*. The introductory story of the present (*paccuppannavatthu*) is set at Jetavana, where the Buddha addresses an incident concerning an elderly monk who was overcome with grief and lamented loudly following the illness and death of a young novice who had faithfully looked after him [Fausböll 1883]. Relating a story of the past, opening with the verse incipit *Agārā paccupetassa*, the Buddha recounts how the Bodhisatta was reborn as the deva king Sakka (Sakra) [Anderson 1978; Fausböll 1883]. When a forest-dwelling hermit succumbed to inconsolable sorrow over the death of his pet fawn, Sakka appeared before him to admonish him against the futility of mourning the dead [Anderson 1978; Fausböll 1883]. In the concluding identification (*samodhāna*), the Buddha explains that the lamenting hermit was the elderly monk, the deceased fawn was the novice, and Sakka was the Bodhisatta himself [Anderson 1978; Fausböll 1883].

  DharmaNexus confirms these connections via automated text-reuse matches, demonstrating an extensive alignment with the *Somadattajātaka* (Ja 410, §1.2–8.1 matching §3.2–10.1 at 0.97 similarity) and near-identical verses shared with Ja 352, Ja 454, Vv 83, Pv 8, Pv 17, Pv 18, and Pv 25 [DharmaNexus]. Textual reuse is also registered in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, *Petavatthu-aṭṭhakathā*, *Vimānavatthu-aṭṭhakathā*, and *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, alongside a cross-language alignment with the Tibetan *Jātakamālā* (D4150) [DharmaNexus].
